sentences.text: The preserved length of the Scipionyx holotype is estimated at just 23.7 cm, representing a small bipedal predator with a long slender neck and elongated hindlimbs.
Its forelimbs were especially elongated, and the skull was large relative to the body, short in shape, and featured very large eye sockets.
The vertebral column likely consists of ten cervical vertebrae and thirteen dorsal vertebrae.
A 2011 study identified eight unique derived traits that distinguish Scipionyx from its closest relatives.
Scipionyx is unique for preserving examples from most major internal organ groups, including blood, vessels, cartilage, muscles, and digestive and respiratory systems.
Scipionyx is one of only two dinosaur fossils with preserved sarcomeres, though Santanaraptor has muscle fibres four times as thick.
The unclosed fontanelle suggests an age limit of about five weeks.
Only one fossil of Scipionyx is known, discovered in 1981 by an amateur paleontologist and introduced to the scientific community in 1993.
The generic name Scipionyx means "Scipio's claw", combining the Latin name Scipio and the Greek word onyx.
Preserved muscle tissue shows exceptional detail, including individual fibres, cells, and subcellular sarcomeres.
Analysis confirmed the red pigment was limonite, a transformation product of original hemoglobin.
Biliverdine, a bile component expected in the liver, was also present in the fossil.
A five millimetre series of food particles indicates the position of Scipionyx's oesophagus.
The holotype specimen provides unique direct information about non-avian dinosaur physiology, specifically regarding digestion, respiration, and ontogenesis.
The shorter-than-expected length of the intestines indicates Scipionyx could process food very efficiently.
Partially digested food found in the fossil's abdomen indicates that Scipionyx ate lizards and fish.
A 2011 study concluded that the liver's exact dimensions and extent could not be determined because it was preserved as a vague halo of body fluids.
Fossil evidence of stomach contents confirms that Scipionyx was a predator.
Scipionyx was considered one of the larger animals within its specific island ecosystem.
Scipionyx was originally assigned to the Coelurosauria group of theropods.
Scipionyx is classified within the family Compsognathidae.
A 2011 study places the phylogenetic position of Scipionyx among the coelurosaurs.
Scipionyx belongs to the parent group Compsognathidae.
Scipionyx was a theropod dinosaur that lived in Italy during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 113 million years ago.
Scipionyx lived during the Albian period in an area that was part of the Apulian Plate and largely covered by the shallow Paratethys sea.
Researchers concluded that Scipionyx generally inhabited small islands formed by dry land amidst shallow marine sediments.
Dal Sasso and Maganuco suggested Scipionyx was likely a recent immigrant from North Africa rather than a permanent resident of the islands for millions of years.
Scipionyx lived during the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.
Scientists have disagreed on how Scipionyx breathed, based on the position of its internal organs.
In 1999, Philip J. Currie hypothesized that tubes on the tail base represented protofeather filaments.
In 2021, Andrea Cau proposed a re-evaluation of Scipionyx's classification and the Compsognathidae group.
